A1-A2.headline: Pelops and the Chariot Race of Ancient Olympia

pages.text:
In old Greek stories, Pelops was a famous king of Pisa.

A large land in southern Greece still carries his name today. At Olympia, people honored him at night. His story helped shape the early Olympic Games.
pages.caption: Roman mosaic with Pelops and Hippodamia

evidence.articleCaption: Roman mosaic with Pelops and Hippodamia, kept in the D. Diogo de Sousa Museum in Braga, Portugal.

pages.text:
Old Greek cities did not tell the exact same story about Pelops's family. Most tales say his father was King Tantalus. Dione or Euryanassa was named as his mother.

Other local stories linked him to the gods Hermes or Atlas or to a leader named Olenus.

Pelops wanted to marry Hippodamia, the daughter of King Oenomaus. The king, fearful of a prophecy, had already killed eighteen suitors in a brutal race. Pelops asked his friend Poseidon for help by the sea. Smiling, the god gave him fast winged horses and a chariot to win.
pages.caption: Pelops and Hippodamia in a bas-relief

evidence.articleCaption: Pelops and Hippodamia racing in a bas-relief (Metropolitan Museum of Art)

pages.text: At Olympia, people built a stone shrine for Pelops near the temple of Zeus. This place marked his famous burial chest. An old writer named Pausanias described special night rites there. Priests gave black rams to Pelops before honoring the great gods. Today, visitors can still see the worn stones.

Long ago, farmers in Greece sometimes dug up giant bones in their fields. People then did not know about huge animals like mammoths. Instead, they believed these giant bones came from great heroes of an older age. Finding such big bones made people trust the Pelops stories even more.

B1-B2.headline: How the Myth of Pelops Shaped the Olympic Games

pages.text:
In Greek myth, Pelops ruled Pisa and gave his name to the Peloponnesus land.

Worshippers honored him at Olympia with solemn night gifts. His hero cult helped shape the early story of the Olympic Games.
pages.caption: Roman mosaic with Pelops and Hippodamia

evidence.articleCaption: Roman mosaic with Pelops and Hippodamia, kept in the D. Diogo de Sousa Museum in Braga, Portugal.

pages.text: Greek writers shared several versions of Pelops's family across different cities. The best-known myth names King Tantalus as his father and Dione or Euryanassa as his mother. Other local myths linked Pelops to quite different figures. Some tied his family to the gods Hermes or Atlas, while another linked him to Olenus.

To marry Hippodamia, Pelops faced King Oenomaus, who had killed eighteen suitors after defeating them in chariot races. Pelops called on Poseidon by the shore, reminding the god of their friendship. The sea god gave him a fast chariot with untamed winged horses.
pages.caption: Pelops and Hippodamia in a bas-relief

evidence.articleCaption: Pelops and Hippodamia racing in a bas-relief (Metropolitan Museum of Art)

pages.text: Near the temple of Zeus at Olympia stood the Pelopion. This stone-ringed shrine marked Pelops's legendary burial chest and drew pilgrims. The writer Pausanias noted that priests offered black rams there at night before honoring the Olympian gods. Worn stone ruins still stand today.

Across ancient Greece, farmers sometimes dug up huge fossil bones in their fields. People then did not know about mammoths or other extinct giant beasts. Instead, locals saw these huge skeletons as real proof of giant heroes from an earlier Heroic Age. Those finds reinforced faith in Pelops and Olympic myths.

C1-C2.headline: Hero Cults, Winged Chariots, and the Legend of Pelops

pages.text: In Hellenic mythology, Pelops reigned over Pisa and bestowed his name upon the Peloponnesus peninsula. Nocturnal rituals honoring his hero cult at Olympia deeply anchored the foundational mythology of the ancient Olympic Games.
pages.caption: Roman mosaic with Pelops and Hippodamia

evidence.articleCaption: Roman mosaic with Pelops and Hippodamia, kept in the D. Diogo de Sousa Museum in Braga, Portugal.

pages.text: Classical traditions preserved divergent genealogies for Pelops across Greek poleis. Canonical narratives identify Tantalus as his father alongside Dione or Euryanassa. Alternative regional lineages associated Pelops with Olympian figures like Hermes and Atlas or Olenus.

Seeking Hippodamia's hand, Pelops confronted King Oenomaus, who had executed eighteen defeated chariot challengers. Invoking Poseidon along the coast, Pelops secured an invincible winged-horse chariot immortalized in ancient relief sculpture.
pages.caption: Pelops and Hippodamia in a bas-relief

evidence.articleCaption: Pelops and Hippodamia racing in a bas-relief (Metropolitan Museum of Art)

pages.text:
The Pelopion at Olympia was a walled sanctuary enclosing the hero's funerary monument. Pausanias documented nocturnal sacrifices of black rams performed there prior to Olympian rites.

Weathered remnants of this ceremonial precinct remain visible.

Throughout antiquity, Greek agriculturalists unearthed fossilized skeletal remains of prehistoric mammoths and extinct megafauna.

Lacking paleontological knowledge, classical communities interpreted these gigantic bones as proof of superhuman ancestors.
